title: Matter
hook: twenty-eight kinds of matter, beginning with the four great elements

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion and wisdom: not traits a person owns, but factors that arise in a moment and pass. Your line: compassion is a moment. Did one arrive yesterday, and did you catch it? Day one thousand eighty-two.

Press a fingertip against the table, or your knee, or the arm of the chair. Something pushes back. It's hard, or soft. It's warm, or cool. Leave the finger there a moment and there's a faint press, a little give, maybe the beat of a pulse. For days now this path has been looking at the mind, factor by factor: what colors a moment, what troubles it, what makes it beautiful. Today the Abhidhamma turns to the other side of its world. The stuff that pushes back. The table, the fingertip, the body doing the pressing. It has one word for all of it, and it begins its list with four.
screen: `PRESS A FINGERTIP DOWN.` → `SOMETHING PUSHES BACK.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The word is rupa: form, or matter. In one sutta the Buddha gives a reason for the name, playing on a verb that means to be afflicted or worn down. It's called rupa, he says, because it gets afflicted: by cold and heat, by hunger and thirst, by flies and mosquitoes, by wind and sun. Matter, in this telling, is the part of you that can be bitten. The Abhidhamma takes that and builds a list. The manual called the Abhidhammattha Sangaha counts twenty-eight kinds of matter, and it begins with four it calls the great elements: earth, water, fire and air. But these aren't soil, rain, flame and wind. They're qualities. Earth is hardness and softness, what pushes back. Water is cohesion, what holds a thing together and lets it flow. Fire is heat, and cold too: a thing's temperature. Air is motion and support, what moves and what keeps something pressed out, the way air keeps a tire firm. Every bit of matter, the manual says, has all four, in different measure. A stone is mostly earth, yet it still holds together, still has a temperature, still presses. And a strange detail: in this system, water can't be touched. Put a hand in a stream, and what touch meets, the Abhidhamma says, is softness, coolness and pressure, which is earth, fire and air. Cohesion is known by the mind, not by the skin. The old suttas use the same four to look at the body: hair and bones as earth, blood and sweat as water, warmth as fire, breath as air. And of every one, the sutta says the same thing: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
screen: `RUPA: WHAT CAN BE BITTEN.` · `FOUR ELEMENTS ARE FOUR QUALITIES.` · `WATER CAN'T BE TOUCHED.` · then, large: `NOT MINE, NOT ME, NOT MY SELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: feel the four, one at a time. Settle where you are. Earth first: the weight of you against the seat, the firmness of the floor under your feet. Then water, which the mind knows rather than the skin: the sense of your body holding together as one shape. Then fire: warmth in your hands, coolness at the tip of the nose. Then air: the breath moving, the chest pressing out and settling back. If attention drifts, begin again at earth. The bell holds the time.
Rupa. Form, matter: the part of the world that can be pressed, warmed, moved and bitten, beginning with four great elements. Today's word.
Your line: four great elements. Today, when you pick up a cup, notice its hardness, its temperature and its weight in your hand before you drink. Day one thousand eighty-two.

howItsDone: In Abhidhamma study, students learn the four great elements as qualities of matter, and in meditation some Theravada traditions teach attending to earth, water, fire and air in the body one by one.

fork.setup: you put your hand into a cool stream. by the Abhidhamma's account, what is your skin actually meeting?
options: softness, coolness and pressure: earth, fire and air
nothing at all: matter isn't real here
fork.reveal: touch meets earth, fire and air. the water element, cohesion, is known by the mind, not by the skin.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: form, matter. one sutta ties the name to a verb for being afflicted.

trapdoor: what you thought: earth, water, fire and air, the stuff of an old chemistry set.
what it means: four qualities in every bit of matter: hardness, cohesion, temperature and motion.
what a scholar hears: the great elements head the manual's list of matter, and touch knows only three of them; cohesion is known by mind alone.
recall: the awakened one, a title, not a name

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 22.79 (Khajjaniya Sutta), why it is called form
Majjhima Nikaya 28 (Mahahatthipadopama Sutta), the four elements in the body
Dhammasangani, Book II (form), the tangible object

notes: Twenty-eight kinds of matter: stated from Abhidhammattha Sangaha VI; confirm.
SN 22.79: the Buddha's wordplay on ruppati (afflicted, 'deformed') and the list cold, heat, hunger, thirst, flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun (creeping things omitted). Paraphrased; confirm.
'Water can't be touched': the tangible object (photthabba) is earth, fire and air in the Dhammasangani and later manuals; cohesion known by mind-door. Confirm phrasing.
MN 28 lists for each element (hair, bones; blood, sweat; warmth; breath) and the refrain 'this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self' are paraphrased, not quoted; confirm.
The tire simile for the air element (distension/support) is the writer's own image.
